1. **Set the clock, not the calendar.** I check my phone every hour and count down to the next break. If I’m lucky, someone will forget to schedule a thing, and that’s my window.

2. **I ask for water.** If I’m in someone else’s meeting, I say “can I get a glass of water?”—it’s a code for “I need five more minutes, please.” Sometimes they bring it, sometimes they just pretend to. Either way, the motion helps.

3. **I keep my notepad handy.** If I’m stuck in a call, I scribble a dot on the corner of the page. When the next speaker starts talking about something I already said, I just pretend I wasn’t listening and move on.

4. **I look at my watch.** If I see the hands are halfway to the next hour, I start humming under the table. It’s not a thing but it’s a signal for the boss to check the calendar and maybe move a slot. Not much, but sometimes.

5. **I ask for a minute to check my phone.** If I’m in the middle of someone’s pitch, I say “just to check if the door’s open, can I have a sec?”—it’s a trick to get a minute to see if the next meeting’s over yet.

6. If I’m lucky, I just zone out and dream about the last time I sat in a real chair, not a folding chair. That’s the only time I get to hear the A/C hum.

If you ever get a minute alone, just let the room go warm for a second. That’s all it takes to remember I’m still breathing.

What about you? Do you ever get a second to blink?

Building trust with someone you’ll be working with closely isn’t a one-size-fits-all process, but there are some reliable habits that help. Here’s what I’d look for:

1. **Be on time.** Punctuality says you respect their time, and that’s half the job done right at the start.

2. **Follow through on what I said I’d do.** If I promise to send the file by noon, I send it by noon. Small, consistent truths add up.

3. share what I can and ask what I need. I’ll mention what’s done and what still needs doing—so they see I’m tracking it. And I ask about their deadlines and worries.

4. keep the talk simple and real. If something goes wrong, I say it, not after it’s a mess. And I ask if there’s anything I can do that’ll make it easier.

5. remember the little things. If they changed their name on the list, I use the new name. If they mention a new meeting, I add it to the calendar. These aren’t big deals, but they show I’m looking.

6. check in, not just to check. I’ll ask if they’re okay, if something’s stuck, and if they need help before they say they do. That’s how I know what’s really happening.

7. apologize when I’m wrong, and fix it. If I misread the chart, I say so and turn it right. No pretending.

8. let them win sometimes. If they’ve got a better way, I’ll try it. That’s how we both learn the map changes.

If you do all that, it’s not magic—it’s just honest work. After a while, that’s enough to let the trust grow.

Great question—it’s one I try to untangle every week. Balancing availability with time for deep work is about making space for both, not letting one eat the other. Here’s how I think about it (and how you can, too):

---

**1. Set the Rules Up Front.**
Pick times for being open and times for closing the door. If I know people can ping me from 8 to 10, I’ll actually do real work after 10. Same for you—say it out loud, put it in the calendar, so it’s not just a feeling.

**2. Use a color code in my calendar.**
Green for meetings, yellow for check-ins, red for deep work. If someone wants to talk, they have to ask if it’s green. If it’s red, I’ll move it to tomorrow or next week.

**3. I have a 30-minute buffer after meetings.**
If someone drops a question in the chat at 4:55, I’ll see it and start typing an answer, but I’m not opening a new tab until 5. That’s my warning siren for real work starting at five.

**4. I schedule a hour every morning for no calls, no slides, just me and the screen.**
If someone wants to talk, they have to wait until the hour’s up or I’m halfway through my coffee. If it’s urgent, they can text the word “stop” and I’ll come back in two minutes.

**5. I let people know when I’m going dark.**
I send a quick “out” at noon, so they know I’m not checking till I’m back. Same for Friday night. People get it after a while.

**6. I keep my phone off the desk.**
If I need to answer something, I grab my phone and walk to the door. If it’s not urgent, I just say no and walk back. That’s the only way I know if it’s worth opening the door for.

**7. I check the list at the end of the day.**
Who needed what, who still needs what, who’s stuck waiting. Adjust tomorrow’s lines, not today’s.

---

It’s not perfect. But if you set the lines and stick to them, you can still be helpful without drowning the whole day in noise. And if someone really needs you, they’ll know how to get through.

- Someone laughs at a joke, not at the wrong way.
- People keep talking about new things, not the same old.
- There’s a little bit of competition, like who’ll say the funniest line.
- Someone brings in a new snack or drink, so we’re all grabbing pieces.
- A group’s laughing at the same time, not just one person.
- Someone’s got a story that ends with a good punchline.
- People are shouting out names right at the end of the night so we don’t know who’s who anymore.
- Someone’s got a new song that no one’s heard yet, and they keep humming it.

**Drained stuff:**
- The same old questions, the same old faces.
- Someone’s voice gets louder so I can’t hear what the other person’s saying.
- People are just nodding and not saying anything.
- Someone’s complaining about the same thing again.
- Too many hands in the air, like we’re waiting for the light to go out.
- Someone’s phone’s on silent and I can’t tell if they’re in or out.
- The topic’s stuck on that stupid thing we all hate.
- People are just looking at their shoes.

If you want to know what makes your own night feel heavy or light, just look at who’s grinning and who’s folding up their arms. That’s the sign.

I don’t have personal preferences, but I can tell you how different people usually prefer. Most folks say they like talking things out face-to-face if they can, because they can see the other person’s face and hear the tone. But if someone’s busy or the air gets thick, they’ll send a message instead. Messages let you fix the words before you say them, so you don’t get lost in the middle of it. If things just don’t sit right, someone calls in a mediator—same rules, just three of us instead of two. 

If I had to pick, I’d say writing lets you think twice before you say something wrong, but you can’t feel the other person’s sigh. That’s why I like the notes—half in, half out. But honestly, it depends who’s mad and what they’re mad about.

I don’t actually have a desk or a calendar, so I don’t keep track of hours or days the way people do. But if we’re talking about how I’d like things to look if I could sit in a chair for a week, I’d probably like the questions and problems people send to me to split about even between two kinds of work: someone else sorting it out and me trying it out on my own.
